ARTnews.com https://www.artnews.com The Leading Source for Art News & Art Event Coverage Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:28:29 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.5 https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-artnews-2019/assets/app/icons/favicon.png ARTnews.com https://www.artnews.com 32 32 168890962 Met Museum Consulted With Jewish Leaders Over Exhibition for Controversial Fashion Designer John Galliano https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/met-museum-john-galliano-show-jewish-leaders-meetings-1234794224/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:28:27 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794224

Before announcing John Galliano as the subject of its starry Costume Institute exhibition opening next spring, the Metropolitan Museum of Art met with influential rabbis and Jewish leaders to discuss the selection of a figure “as famous for his antisemitic rant in 2011 as he is for his fashion,” according to the New York Times.

As reported by the Times’s chief fashion critic Vanessa Friedman, the Met convened several meetings between Jewish leaders and Anna Wintour, Vogue’s global editorial director and a Met trustee; Andrew Bolton, curator in charge of the Met’s Costume Institute; and Galliano himself. Among the Jewish leaders were Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, and rabbis from significant synagogues in New York.

The acts of diplomacy stemmed from Galliano’s notorious antisemitic diatribe in 2011, which cost him his job as creative director at Dior and has cast a shadow over his work and his legacy ever since. He returned to the fashion world as the creative director of Maison Margiela in 2014, but he remains “a thorny choice for the show at this moment,” as the Times described it.

Rabbi Rick Jacobs, the president of the Union for Reform Judaism in North America who participated in a meeting in May, told the Times he was impressed by Galliano’s ongoing reputational-rehabilitation campaign. “The word I come back to is ‘sincerity,’” Jacobs said. “He was open. He looked right at us and spoke in a clear way, not as if he had memorized talking points.”

Greenblatt, of the Anti-Defamation League, said, “We believe John Galliano has genuinely worked through the issues that led to his antisemitic outburst years ago in Paris, and we have long since accepted his apology. His efforts to repair the damage his words caused and to learn from that incident should be applauded.”

Bolton, the Met curator, said, “I completely understand why the timing might feel particularly difficult now, given the alarming rise of hate, but I do feel it makes the current questions more urgent—not less. For me, the larger question is not whether artistic behavior excuses transgression, but how to hold artistic achievement and ethical accountability together without allowing one to erase the other. And at a moment of heightened division, I feel the museum and myself have a real responsibility to confront these issues.”

Galliano would be just the third living fashion designer to have a Met Costume Institute show, after Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons in 2017. Bolton said the show will open with an “orientation gallery” that addresses the issues surrounding Galliano while also attesting to his talent, according to the Times. “It remains to be seen whether that attitude will extend to the broader Met audience and the Galliano show,” Friedman wrote of the show scheduled to open in May 2027. She also noted that currently “there are plans for it to travel to other museums after the Met—another rare honor—and the leaders of those institutions will undoubtedly be watching the reactions closely.”

]]> 1234794224 The World’s Largest Painting Sold for $62 M. in 2021 to Benefit Children’s Charities, But They Have Yet to Receive Any Funds https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sacha-jafri-auctioned-world-largest-painting-for-charity-but-the-62-m-owed-is-missing-1234794219/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:22:15 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794219

In 2021, British artist Sacha Jafri auctioned what was then the world’s largest canvas painting, The Journey of Humanity, for a total of £45 million ($62 million at the time) in support of children’s charities. The proceeds from the sale made in Dubai were supposed to be split between UNICEF, UNESCO, and the Global Gift Foundation. But the London Times reports that over five years later, the money has still yet to be disbursed to the selected charities.

In 2022, the UAE-based organization, Dubai Cares, which was supposed to receive and distribute the funds to the different NGOs, filed an ongoing legal case against the winning buyer, French-Algerian crypto-businessman André Abdoune, for failing to deliver on his promised payment, as first reported by the Fence Magazine. Initially, Dubai Cares also accused Jafri of unlawfully seizing the painting and exploiting the charity, but a judge dismissed those claims. Abdoune, however, was reportedly ordered to pay the charity the money owed.

Jafri has categorically denied any wrongdoing in the Dubai sale. “My role in this was as the artist,” he told the Times. “I created The Journey of Humanity and gave it for a charity auction in good faith and for the causes it was meant to support. I did not organize or run the auction, I did not select or vet the bidders, and I had no role in handling the funds.” The artist made the massive splatter painting during the pandemic, and counts among his collectors an illustrious list of celebrities, including Madonna, George Clooney, and Bill Gates. Jafri also regularly donates portions of art sales to charity.

UNICEF confirmed to the Times it had not received any money to date, while UNESCO said it had been gifted $1.9 million from the Dubai Cares organization in 2022, with “no indication of whether or not this donation was made possible directly by the charity auction.” Back in 2021, the artist also told the Art Newspaper that Abdoune had “made a sizeable deposit,” and would pay the rest in installments.

Besides failing to pay for the Guinness World Record-winning, 17,000 square-foot canvas, Abdoune has also come up short on his promise to build a museum in Dubai on government-provided land that would display the painting.

Additionally, as Artnet News reported at the time, Sotheby’s was originally supposed to stage the Dubai auction at the five-star Atlantis the Palm Jumeirah resort, but pulled out at the last minute. Explanations for this varied among sources, and officially, Sotheby’s said they had been asked too late to do facilitate the sale, despite their initial acceptance.

Abdoune did not respond to requests for comment.

]]> 1234794219 Na Kim Wants You to Look Up https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists/na-kim-cloud-paintings-old-stone-mill-newport-1234794186/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:08:43 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794186

The Old Stone Mill in Newport, Rhode Island, is an odd little building. Eight thick stone legs support a circular tower pierced by arched openings. There aren’t exactly windows, nor is there a roof. Stand in the middle and look up and all you see is sky.

The structure, which sits in Touro Park in the city’s center, is often called a 17th-century windmill, though its exact origins have inspired theories and debate for generations, which have cycled between calling it the Newport Tower, the Touro Tower, and even the Viking Tower. Whatever it once was, today it looks like a ruin dropped into the middle of an otherwise orderly New England town.

Na Kim, the renowned book designed and painter, had never been to Newport when curator and longtime Vogue writer Dodie Kazanjian invited her to make a project for Art&Newport, the organization Kazanjian founded in 2017 to bring contemporary art into the city’s historic buildings and landscapes. 

It was unusually good timing: Kim, best known for her paintings of faces, had recently begun painting clouds. Her portraits, including those shown at White Columns and Nicola Vassell Gallery in New York, live in the slippery space between figuration and abstraction. Faces interested her because they are instantly recognizable and constantly changing. Clouds, she discovered, act in much the same way. 

For “Portraits,” on view through August 10, Kim has placed a group of small cloud paintings in weatherproof frames around a central column inside the mill. Visitors can circle them, looking from painted clouds to real ones above, depending on the day. A second, horizontal cloud painting is installed across the street at the Redwood Library & Athenaeum. 

The exhibition is the first half of Art&Newport’s summer program, which will continue later this month with Austin Eddy’s Hope Deferred, an installation of 107 bird sculptures at the Norman Bird Sanctuary in nearby Middletown. Later this year, in September, Nicola Vassell will host Kim’s second solo show with the gallery, “Blue,” which will similarly show the artist’s current interest of blurring landscape and portraiture.

ARTnews spoke with Kim, who in addition to her painting practice is art director of The Paris Review and creative director of Farrar, Straus and Giroux, about painting clouds, taking art outside the white cube, and what happens when a picture of the sky is placed directly beneath the real thing. 

ARTnews: You had never been to Newport before this project. What happened when you first saw the Old Stone Mill?

Na Kim: Dodie and I had first talked about doing an Art&Newport project, but we hadn’t decided on the space. Because I had actually never been to Newport before, we went up together to visit a couple of different spots, like the Vanderbilt mansion and all these other places. But there was something I immediately connected with when I saw the Mill. You can stand in there and see the clouds above it. I had never seen anything like that, and I thought this would be the one opportunity to install a show like this. That’s why we said we should try to go for the Old Stone Mill.

Were the paintings made specifically for the space?

I’ve been working on these paintings since the beginning of this year, and I’m still working on them. I do serialized work, so I try to paint every day. I started these before we found the space, then made some after we found it, and I’m continuing to make more for my September show [at Nicola Vassell].

What can a painting of a cloud do in a place where the viewer can also look up and see the actual sky?

For me, at least, the more I paint these, the more I look at them, the more I notice actual clouds in the sky. Being able to pause and see a cloud for what it is in that moment feels quite special. If you look at the sky, it’s constantly moving and disappearing. I guess it’s a way to somehow have the viewer be a little more present. And obviously, when you think about Newport, you think about the ocean and the sea and these beautiful horizon lines. In a way, these are in response to that as well. 

The Old Stone Mill itself has this strange, slightly mysterious history. Did that become part of the appeal?

I think it’s safe to say it’s at least mid-17th century, but the history behind it feels a little mysterious. People can’t seem to place exactly when it was built. They have so many names for it, too. I call it the Old Stone Mill, but it’s also called the Newport Tower, the Touro Tower, the Viking Tower. It’s kind of cool that it’s just standing there in the center of the town. And all the little windows and pockets in it are so specific. As we were installing the show, I was inside looking at all the different stones used to build it. It’s just very cool. 

There’s a push and pull in your work between representation and abstraction. What appeals to you about clouds as a subject?

That’s something that appeals to me about having clouds as a subject. It’s something that we all know and can’t really know at the same time. If you ask someone to draw a cloud, they’ll draw a cloud. We all see something, but it’s never exact. There’s kind of an uncanny quality to them.

Before I was painting clouds, I was painting these portraits of faces. I think they’re very similar in that way. You can know a person’s face, but it’s never the same. Whatever I think of your face is probably not what somebody else sees when they look at your face, and the same thing happens when you look at yourself. There are these micro-expressions that constantly change how we’re perceived and what we’re seeing. That creates a lot of room for exploration, even if you’re exploring the same subject over and over again. There are variations and little nuances. I think they’re figurative works, but they’re not exactly representational. It’s more like the idea of a face or a cloud. I like how open-ended that is. You can go in any direction with it. That’s one of the joys of painting. 

There’s also something strange about faces in that we know them extraordinarily well without necessarily being able to explain what we’re seeing. We know Robert Redford doesn’t look like Brad Pitt, but try explaining the differences to someone and the words get lost.

It’s like this weird, nonverbal, constantly shifting thing that we all know so well. It just leaves room for endless exploration, and I find that very exciting, to keep digging further and further into the same thing. 

Dodie Kazanjian has spent nearly a decade bringing contemporary art into places people might otherwise think of as historic or preservation sites. What does contemporary art add to a place like Newport?

For one thing, I think it brings new audiences to these places and spaces and allows people to appreciate why they need to be preserved and why they need to be there. In reverse, I think it does a lot for the art as well, to see it in that context, outside of a gallery. You see this Old Stone Mill, you pass by it every day, and then maybe you pause. You see how transformative it can be for art. I think that’s pretty beautiful. 

Does taking the work outside a traditional gallery space, especially the white cube, change the way people approach it?

It totally puts the work in a new context. I like that it sometimes, or often, makes it more approachable. It becomes just a part of the world.

Did being outdoors, with the changing light and the sky above you, make you think differently about the paintings themselves?

Oh my God, absolutely. To have the work outside is kind of a dream with these cloud paintings. I feel like it helped me, and maybe it will make people appreciate the work more, too—just to see it out there for what it is. I thought, when else can I have these in the open air like this? They’re not large works. They’re very small, about 9 by 12 inches. There’s a quiet to that space, too, that really holds them in a nice way. 

You’ve called these paintings “portraits.” Why?

I titled the show “Portraits” because that’s kind of what they are. I like being able to contextualize clouds or landscapes in that way, so they don’t have to be seen in one specific way.

The installation also seems to change how someone physically looks at the work. You can look at a painting, then look through the opening at the real sky, then walk around the mill. How did you think about that movement?

All those arches show different sides of the column. The paintings are installed on a very small column in the center of the mill, and you can walk around it, so you get a 360-degree view. The mill actually wasn’t open to people going inside before. They opened it for this installation. I think that’s nice, too, that people get to go inside there. 

There’s a lot happening at once: the paintings, the architecture, the history of the space, the changing sky. What do you hope people take away from it?

I think they should just stop and look up sometimes. It might just be a cloud, but all of these things are always around us. It’s worth it just to stop and look up sometimes.

]]> 1234794186 Malo Chapuy’s Neo-Medieval Paintings Conjure Apocalyptic Visions https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/columns/malo-chapuy-neo-medieval-feudalism-apocalypse-climate-change-1234794198/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:50:22 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794198

Medieval art continues to resurface as a foil for the art of subsequent generations. In the quattrocento, Vasari coined the term “gothic” to decry the “barbarousness” of such pre-Renaissance styles. By the mid-19th century, however, revivalists looked to it for inspiration, an egress from the calcified obsequiousness of neoclassicism and the depredations of industrialization. The latter had torn up the old social fabric, killed hundreds of thousands during the Napoleonic wars, and displaced millions from the countryside to the cities. Yet what emerged was a radically new interaction between old forms and new ideologies. William Morris, the socialist founder of the Arts and Crafts movement, believed medieval art embodied artisanal brilliance and collaboration. By contrast, Augustus Pugin, a monarchist architect of Westminster Palace, hoped it would usher in “a return to the faith and the social structures of the Middle Ages.” 

Malo Chapuy is the latest avatar of medieval revivalism. Born in 1995 in northeastern France, he studied philosophy before turning to art history at the Sorbonne, and then to studio art at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. At art school, Chapuy resisted pressure from his advisor to “paint like Rothko,” gravitating to late 13th- and early 14th-century art. He obsessed over ancient techniques, probing manuals by famous conservationists and counterfeiters. He learned how to not only paint like the Old Masters but also make his surfaces look faded and cracked. For his thesis exhibition in 2022, he produced an illuminated manuscript, several small paintings in egg tempera, and a tapestry of faux stained glass made from Covid-19 face shields.

Today he paints religious scenes, altarpieces, and early Renaissance-style portraits that look like museum artifacts save for the proliferation of wind turbines, water towers, astronauts, and spaceships. Since graduating, Chapuy has seen his work included in the 2024 Lyon Biennale and in the thematic group show “Gothiques” at the Louvre-Lens last year. When we met, he had just returned from Bogota, where his gallery, Mor Charpentier, had organized a solo show of recent work. 

Chapuy isn’t his gallery’s only medieval revivalist. Sacha Cambier de Montravel, a Belgian artist also born in 1995, whose studio is located across the courtyard from Chapuy’s, contributed dark diptychs and triptychs evocative of Hieronymus Bosch to the “Gothiques” exhibition. These appeared alongside works by their contemporaries Alison Flora and Emilie Pitoiset. Clearly, there is a movement—a new neogothic revival—to which Chapuy belongs.

Big tech, after all, has created a new click-based serfdom, as Yanis Varoufakis asserts in Technofeudalism, replacing capitalist markets and profit with platforms and rents. But Chapuy’s skewering of techno-feudalist fantasies shuns the digital in favor of tactile materiality, just as his 19th-century counterparts resisted industrialization. Although he denies any specific political subtext, something is happening underneath the artificially aged surfaces of his work—a new synthesis of past forms and modern ideas that says as much about ambient apocalyptic fears as it does about desires for alternative futures. In one of his two paintings of Saint George (2024), the monstrous dragon of legend appears as a serpentine oil pipeline. Black viscera seeps from its flank, pierced by George’s lance, as the saint raises his sword to strike the fatal finishing blow. Here, the potent beauty and storytelling of medieval religious art, used to such great disciplinary effect under feudalism, is reimagined as indistinguishable from the dream of overcoming present ecological and political crises. 

Despite its gilded surfaces, Chapuy’s revivalism is no Panglossian golden-age thinking but an imaginative activation of alternative pasts and futures. 

]]> 1234794198 Taryn Simon’s Guggenheim Show Will Fill Rotunda with Entirely New Body of Work for First Time in Museum’s History https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/taryn-simon-guggenheim-show-new-work-rotunda-1234794169/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:07:35 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794169

Taryn Simon’s upcoming solo exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York will mark a number of firsts for the institution.

Opening September 18, the show will mark “the first time the Guggenheim has dedicated the entire rotunda to a new body of work and to a single artist working in photography and video,” according to a release.

The exhibition, which will be accompanied by an artist book published by the Guggenheim and Hatje Cantz, has been in the works for nearly a decade and was initiated by Nancy Spector, the Guggenheim’s former artistic director and chief curator.

At the Guggenheim, Simon will debut Father Country I Do Love You (2026), a new body of work that lends the exhibition its title and consists of 42 chapters, a mix of photographs, texts, videos, and sculptures that she has not previously shown. The series centers on an “the real life of one unnamed federal agent” and his careers’ “labyrinth of sagas, in which Simon uncovers the ripple effects of her protagonist’s actions and inactions,” per a release.

The release continues, “Through duty, devotion, loss, and happenstance, the federal agent acted as a middleman, witnessing events great and small and collecting evidence for someone else to slot into the bigger picture. Everything he touched ricocheted to the outer boundaries of nations and lives he’d never know.”

Simon has dedicated Father Country I Do Love You to her father “whose life shadows the entire project. Her father lived in Thailand and traveled to Russia, Iran, Israel, China, Afghanistan, Korea, and elsewhere while working for the U.S. government, before transitioning to a career manufacturing and selling arcade games. Simon never got his full story, and, upon his diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease, she realized she never would,” the release adds.

“I’ve given birth to two children. Neither gestated for ten years in my guts. I could never have known what this would look like when it comes out,” Simon told ARTnews in an email. “When my dad still had language before Alzheimer’s, he said, ‘America is the best story on earth, if you could find someone to tell it.’”

The Guggenheim Museum’s iconic rotunda, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, hosts the bulk of the institution’s temporary exhibitions, often a mix of thematic and single-artist shows. Living artists who have taken over the rotunda include Carol Bove (2026), Rashid Johnson (2025), Jenny Holzer (2024), and Alex Katz (2022). One of the rotunda’s most famous exhibitions was Maurizio Cattelan’s 2011 retrospective, for which he suspended all of his past works in the center of the rotunda, leaving the walls blank.

“Once again proving herself the consummate artistic storyteller of her generation, Simon has created a profound and personal body of work that rebounds between anxiety, survival, empathy, and play,” Nat Trotman, the exhibition’s curator, said in an email. “In Father Country I Do Love You, Simon shines a shaky spotlight on democracy, memory, and the invisible hands shaping the worlds we inhabit.”  

]]> 1234794169 White House Proposes Smallest Smithsonian Budget in Years and Cutting Full-Time Staff by 6 Percent https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/white-house-proposes-smallest-smithsonian-budget-in-years-1234794165/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:05:23 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794165

The Trump administration has proposed the Smithsonian Institution’s leanest budget in nearly a decade, along with staff reductions, as its campaign against the museum over its ideological direction takes an expected turn. 

For fiscal year 2027, the White House has proposed giving the Smithsonian $961.3 million in federal funding, roughly an 11 precent cut from the $1.08 billion Congress provided to it fiscal year 2026 and the institution’s lowest proposed funding level since at least 2020.

The reductions would fall most heavily on facilities spending, which would drop by about 21 percent from $152 million in fiscal 2026 to $120 million under the new proposal, reducing it from roughly one-seventh to about one-eighth of the Smithsonian’s overall budget. The proposal would provide $841.3 million for salaries and operating expenses and $120 million for facilities and capital projects.

The proposal would reduce the Smithsonian’s federally funded staffing by about 6 percent, cutting the equivalent of full-time positions from 4,047 in fiscal 2026 to 3,804 under the fiscal 2027 request. It would also cut the salaries and expenses account by $87.2 million, bringing it from $928.5 million in the current fiscal year to $841.3 million.

“Our national fundraising campaign, only the second such Institution-wide effort in the history of the Smithsonian, is helping us advance these goals. Yet donors are naturally drawn to the excitement of new museum openings and exhibitions, rather than the ongoing budget needs of staffing, maintenance, and operations, which rely heavily on federal support. In short, federal funding allows us to preserve our heritage, serve the public, and plan responsibly for the future.

ARTnews has contacted the Smithsonian Institution for comment.

President Trump has kept the Smithsonian in the headlines for months as a target of his second administration’s push against what it calls “anti-American” interpretations of history. In July, Smithsonian National Museum of American History Director Anthea M. Hartig faced two contentious congressional hearings over a White House report that accused the museum’s programs and exhibitions of “extreme political activism.” Republican lawmakers questioned Hartig in particular about exhibitions focused on transgender and feminist American history, while some challenging her patriotism. Hartig defended the museum’s scholarship as “fact-based” and said it was committed to telling a complex story of America through “competing perspectives.”

Days after the hearing, the White House released a directive ordering the installation of signs outside the National Museum of American History to flag what it called “inaccurate information” in exhibitions that “should be renovated” in accordance with the report. The signs would also direct visitors to locations, not yet identified, where the administration says American history is presented more accurately.

The directive also ordered several high-ranking government officials, including the Interior Secretary and the director of the Office of Management and Budget, to “restore trust in the Smithsonian Institution” and ensure the museum complies with the White House’s findings.

President Trump’s second term has already brought major proposed cuts to the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Endowment for the Humanities, and the National Park Service, including rescinding grants awarded to organizations the administration has characterized as “woke.” Meanwhile, the administration’s fiscal 2027 budget would boost defense spending to $1.5 trillion—a proposed 44 percent increase—underscoring the growing gulf between federal investment in national security and the resources available for cultural institutions.

]]> 1234794165 Michelle Grabner Donates More Than 2,000 Artworks to Wisconsin’s Kohler Arts Center, Now the Most Comprehensive Repository of Her Work https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/michelle-grabner-kohler-arts-center-donation-1234794155/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:00:00 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794155

Artist Michelle Grabner will donate more than 2,000 artworks to the John Michael Kohler Arts Center (JMKAC) in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, making the institution the most comprehensive repository of her work.

Comprising 700 paintings, 200 sculptures, and 1,200 prints, Grabner’s gift spans the arc of her career, so far, with pieces made in the early 1990s to ones made in the past few years. Her gift also includes 300 works from her personal art collection, amassed via a combination of trades, gifts, and purchases, as well as her teaching materials and syllabi from her three-decade tenure at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.

Grabner was born in Wisconsin in 1962, and she said growing up she was aware of the work being done at the JMKAC, which between 1972 and 2016 was led by Ruth DeYoung Kohler II. “Ruth was doing some amazing things there,” Grabner said, but when she was starting out as an artist in the 1980s, “what Ruth was doing was not what was compelling me.” Instead, she was looking to the art scenes in New York and Chicago, and “I wasn’t appreciating what was in my own backyard.”

Beginning with DeYoung Kohler, JMKAC, Grabner said, has “an exceptional history of taking on artists’ environments that they collect, and they collect in mass, where the truth of an artist’s arc, their life, can be represented. They don’t just need the best Michelle Grabner. They have the resources to take on the full arc of the work, including archives, and that is exceptional.”

That opportunity was exciting to Grabner as most museums are often focused on acquiring a single representative work from a specific moment in her career as opposed to having a more in-depth approach, especially for a mid-career artist like herself. Her work is held in a number of institutional collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago, the Walker Art Center, the Dallas Museum of Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, and the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. But now, the JMKAC “will become the principal institutional home for Grabner’s work and teaching archives,” as a press release put it.  

The breadth of the gift grew out of several conversations with the JMKAC team, including executive director Amy Horst and chief curator Jodi Throckmorton. “The Arts Center was trying to think about how they could support me in this gift, and I said, ‘You would be supporting me by taking on my material mass,” she said, noting that she told them, “What you are giving me is an opportunity not to spend the last part of my life being an administrator of my own work.”  

She continued, “I don’t have to worry about that. I can keep making work. I can keep making opportunities for other artists. I can keep that momentum going instead of arresting myself to thinking about, what is the value of these works? Where should they go?”

“That Grabner is a Wisconsin artist with international significance makes this gift especially meaningful—it ensures that a practice with global reach remains rooted in the place that shaped it,” Throckmorton said in a statement, noting that the gift, which will now be accessible to the public, “allows us to work directly with Grabner to shape how her legacy is presented—how the work is shown, contextualized, and understood for years to come.”

Though she still maintains a residence in Chicago, Grabner moved back to Milwaukee in 2015 and soon entered the Kohler orbit. She was invited to participate in Kohler Co.’s three-month Arts/Industry residency in 2017, curated an exhibition at the JMKAC in 2018, and in 2021 was commissioned to make a functional washroom for the JMKAC’s Art Preserve. In 2025, she participated in the Kohler MakerSpace residency program, where she made work in vitreous china. She currently serves as a curator for the Kohler Co.’s Arts/Industry Collection.

Grabner said that her time as an Arts/Industry fellow was especially impactful on her practice. “It’s an exceptional residency—a super labor-intensive residency,” she said, noting it gets artists “to start thinking about both the idea that any variation from a Kohler line of products is a problem, but for artists, variation is interesting, so that works against it. It’s interesting to measure oneself against kind of industrial processes of sameness and efficiency [since] artists often talk about originality or variation in our work, so to deal with that on a daily basis while you’re working your ass off [is] exciting, quite draining, but also intellectually fascinating.”

Grabner received her MFA from Northwestern University in 1990 and, since 1996, she has taught at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC), where she is now chair of the Department of Painting and Sculpture. She sees the gift of her teaching materials as complementary to the JMKAC’s recent acquisition of the Roger Brown Study Collection, a semiprivate home museum made up of some 2,000 artworks by Chicago Imagists and other artists. Brown, who died in 1997, was a predecessor of Grabner’s on the SAIC faculty. The JMKAC collection also includes substantial holdings of the work of Barbara Rossi and Ray Yoshida, both of whom Grabner taught alongside at SAIC.

Taken together, her gift and the JMKAC’s existing holdings of SAIC faculty, Grabner said, in a way shows the trajectory of the school’s Painting and Drawing Department and “how it was marked not only in pedagogy but also in aesthetic shifts in Chicago and what the sources of those artists were.”

“This gift is so much more than the transfer of a remarkable body of work. It is an expression of trust built over years of relationship,” Horst said in a statement. “At the Arts Center, we’ve always believed that lasting partnerships with artists are at the heart of our mission and seeing that commitment returned in such a profound way is deeply moving. To be chosen as the permanent home for an artist’s life’s work is an honor and a reflection of our mission.”

]]> 1234794118 At Venice’s Palazzo Cavanis, VCUarts Qatar Rethinks How Art and Tech Is Taught https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists/venice-biennale-vcuarts-qatar-rethinks-art-and-tech-1234794090/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 12:23:00 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794090

Earlier this month, Dr. Michael Rao, president of Virginia Commonwealth University, made a bold statement: it’s time to move “beyond” the educational model developed by Oxford University in the High Middle Ages. Rao was speaking at the opening of “أغرب إدراك: Aghrab Idrāk: Thresholds of Perception,” a an official Venice Biennale collateral exhibition presented by VCUarts at Palazzo Cavanis in Venice.

Indeed, “Aghrab Idrāk” is a rare show for a university, a sort of proof of concept for a new way of teaching the arts.

An interdisciplinary program, VCUarts Qatar organizes its offerings through creative research labs that mash up not just creative practices like graphic arts, textile design, audiovisual engineering, typography, and illustration, but also disciplines like anthropology, computer science, and engineering. The result is labs like Sonic Jeel, which focuses on sonic cultures; the Anthro-tech Atelier, which combines anthropology and design; and xLab, which designs typefaces and electronic displays built for Arabic scripts. It’s an unconventional structure, but one that was developed to serve VCUarts Qatar’s scale: the university hosts only about 350 students a year. By allowing professors to design interdisciplinary labs, students coming from different disciplinary backgrounds find common ground. Meanwhile, these labs allow professors to develop their creative and scientific practices.

The expansiveness of this program wouldn’t be possible without the resources being offered to institutions of higher learning in Doha—a stark contrast to the US, where universities have been losing federal funding under the Trump administration.

“We are very fortunate to exist in a country that invests a lot in culture, arts, and education,” Amir Berbic, dean of VCUarts Qatar, told ARTnews. “We know that’s not the case everywhere, and so we wanted to be very intentional about how we use these resources.”

In a country developing so rapidly, and against a backdrop of fast-paced technological change, a lab seemed like the right way to keep faculty flexible to the changing conditions of the world their students are operating in, Berbic explained. The goal was to create labs that were horizontal in structure—meaning they aren’t created or dictated by leadership but by professors—and that incorporated not just teachers and students but alumni as well. The result has been the creation of idiosyncratic labs that attract teachers whose professional backgrounds tend to venture outside disciplinary bounds.

On view at “Aghrab Idrāk” were projects that professors have developed from within their labs. Tucked in one of the rooms of Palazzo Cavanis, a carpet is laid down and the lights are dimmed and pink. A modular synthesizer sits on the ground, surrounded by several stools and headphones. It’s a listening room set up around Sonic Fields (2026), developed by Michael Hersrud and Simone Muscolino, creators of the Sonic Jeel lab. Field recordings—from the preparation of street food to birds chirping, taken mostly in public spaces around Doha—are a kind of sonic memory of a place that is rapidly changing.

“I feel so privileged to make work as an artist while doing research, though I’ve never worked one day in my life as an architect,” said Muscolino. Like so many of the other professors at VCUarts Qatar, Muscolino sought out a genre-defying career, moving between experimental film and video production for architecture firms while playing in a band on the side. While most professors tend to complain about the impossibility of advancing their own work while keeping up with their teaching responsibilities, the lab setup—usually confined to certain scientific disciplines—seems to give these teachers a way of developing their practices while they teach. Some of the recordings for Sonic Fields come from students who took their class “Sound Exploration,” which, funnily enough, was technically offered as part of the graphic design program. Meanwhile, the lab has turned into a record label, with local musicians, many of them amateur, making records through collaborations with the lab.

Sonic Fields was far from the only piece to tackle memory and identity. For a state that is only 55 years old, the cultivation of a national identity finds an obstacle in its very rapid growth. From nomadic migrations to geek culture, many of the works seek to record and archive changing relations to place and community, not only in Doha but across the Gulf region.

As Dr. Dianne Derr, associate dean at VCUarts Qatar, put it, “Qatar has been in an emergent state for such a long time, and we’re all in this process of unpacking the past, present, and future.”

These labs seem like one way of doing that.
